author: BrentDesk Staff
headline: Energy performance contracting depends on an agreed baseline
deck: A model that pays the contractor from the savings it delivers has obvious appeal in Saudi buildings, and one persistent obstacle.
excerpt: Energy performance contracting offers a route to funding building efficiency in Saudi Arabia, but depends on agreeing a consumption baseline neither party can verify independently.
content:
Energy performance contracting is among the mechanisms a Saudi facilities management market might reasonably adopt, and it will be in scope at the Saudi Facility Management Association's forum in Riyadh from 20 September, themed on smart facilities and smart cities.

The model is straightforward in principle. A contractor identifies efficiency measures in a building, funds and installs them, and is paid from the resulting reduction in energy cost over an agreed period. The client gets improvements without capital outlay; the contractor gets a return proportional to the savings delivered. It converts an efficiency programme from a capital decision into an operating one, which is why it exists.

Saudi buildings are good candidates. Cooling dominates consumption, much of the existing stock was built when energy was cheap and specified accordingly, and the measures available — chiller replacement, controls, variable speed drives, lighting, building envelope improvements — have well-documented savings. Historically low electricity tariffs weakened the case, and tariff reform has strengthened it.

The obstacle is the baseline. Payment depends on measuring savings, and savings are the difference between actual consumption and what consumption would have been without the intervention. The second figure is counterfactual and cannot be measured, only estimated from historical data adjusted for weather, occupancy and use. Every element of that adjustment is negotiable, and both parties have a direct financial interest in the outcome.

Where historical data is thin or unreliable — a common position in buildings without sub-metering — establishing a credible baseline is genuinely difficult, and disputes about it are the most frequent cause of these arrangements failing. Internationally recognised measurement and verification protocols exist precisely to address this, and they require instrumentation that many buildings do not have.

Which is where the forum's stated theme becomes relevant rather than decorative. Sensors, sub-metering and building analytics produce the consumption data that makes a defensible baseline possible. The technology's value in this application is not optimisation but evidence — it makes performance contracting bankable by making savings verifiable.

The Saudi context adds a further consideration. A large share of the building stock is government or quasi-government owned, and public sector procurement rules are not always compatible with a contract that pays a private party from future savings. Where that has been resolved elsewhere it has generally required specific enabling frameworks.

The association's forum disclosure remains limited: no agenda, speakers, exhibitors or sponsors had been published, and its website still shows the 2025 edition.

This publication has covered the Saudi FM sector's move from preventive to predictive maintenance and the technology stack behind it.
